newsitem.title: ZAIRE: New Hutu exodus as West ponders Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: New Hutu exodus as West ponders Zaire force.

text.p: Rwandan refugees have started streaming towards their homeland from Zaire, in what appears to be a second exodus that could remove the need for a planned U.N. force intended to help them.

Zaire, which says a multinational force is still vital, on Wednesday suspended its army chief for breaking ranks and arguing against U.N. intervention, in a potentially dangerous split in the country's hierarchy.

Canada said most nations involved in the humanitarian crisis in eastern Zaire believed a military force was still needed to deliver aid to more than a million Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans wandering the bush after fleeing fighting between the Zaire army and ethnic Tutsi rebels.
But Ottawa's Deputy Foreign Minister Gordon Smith said military planners needed to develop a range of options -- including not sending ground troops at all.
Smith spoke at a news conference after a series of meetings at the United Nations, one of which involved representatives from 60 countries, including states who volunteered troops.
"Virtually all countries, including Zaire...believe that a military force is still required," he said.

"The conclusions of the meetings today are that the military planners need to develop options," Smith said. "The options of course include a zero option -- that there is no need for a military force to provide security to humanitarian relief organisations."

The special U.N. envoy who has been negotiating a mandate for a multinational force openly questioned whether a strong force would now be needed. France and Spain maintained their support for a strong force, projected to total 10,000.
"The more refugees coming into Rwanda, of course the less need for a strong military intervention," envoy Raymond Chretien told reporters in the Zaire capital Kinshasa.

The U.N.'s World Food Programme said as many as 100,000 Hutu refugees were on the road, possibly the start of a second mass exodus to the homeland they fled in panic after the Rwandan genocide and civil war in 1994.

"There are strong indications that a large movement of people from the Bukavu area are heading north towards Goma. We believe there could be more than 100,000," WFP spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie said in Nairobi.
She said a U.N. assessment team had been allowed into Bukavu by Zairean rebels late on Wednesday, but had so far been unable to give more precise reports.
Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young said hundreds of thousands of refugees appeared to be heading through toward the Rwandan border in a new mass exodus.

"Information we have seems to indicate strongly enough that hundreds of thousands more that might still be in the region are on their way from the southern part of the eastern region of Zaire towards Bukavu to return to Rwanda," he said.
About 700,000 Hutus are thought to be still in Zaire after 500,000 walked back into Rwanda from Goma between November 15 and 19.

Hundreds of thousands of refugees have returned to Rwanda to escape war pitting Zairean rebels supported by Rwanda against soldiers from Rwanda's Hutu-dominated former army and Hutu militias who led the 1994 genocide of Rwanda's minority Tutsis.
Western aid chiefs, donors and relief agencies will meet in Geneva on Saturday to coordinate aid plans for the refugees, with their action now expected to be largely based in Rwanda.
On Wednesday authorities suspended Zaire's outspoken army chief of staff General Eluki Monga for saying a multinational force was no longer needed in Zaire.
"General Eluki has been suspended because of the declarations he made," government spokesman Boguo Makeli said.
Eluki told French radio on Tuesday that the intervention of a U.N. force was now unnecessary and repeated complaints by the army that the government was not giving it the means to battle rebels.
The Zaire government maintains a multinational force is still needed to help refugees and displaced Zaireans. It also wants such a force to help it recover territory from rebels.

As chief of staff of the armed forces, estimated at more than 50,000 men, Eluki was regarded as one of the four most powerful generals. However his ragged army, poorly trained and ill-disciplined, proved unable to withstand the advance of Rwandan-backed rebels in the east of the country.
